content.text: 📖 Reading Note: Tuples are preferred over lists for geographic coordinates because coordinates should never be accidentally modified. If you store Bengaluru's centroid as lalbagh_park = (12.9507, 77.5848), using a tuple prevents code like lalbagh_park[0] = 99.0 from silently corrupting your spatial analysis. In GIS programming, coordinate pairs are almost always represented as tuples for this immutability guarantee.

content.text: Importance: Efficient handling of large datasets, simplifies cleaning and transformation.

📖 Reading Note: Pandas GroupBy is one of the most powerful tools for urban analysis. Example: After loading Chennai's water supply data (daily readings from all 200 zones for 3 years), a single line — df.groupby('zone')['supply_liters'].mean() — computes the average daily water supply for each zone. Planners instantly see which zones are under-served (< 135 LPCD standard). Without Pandas, this would require complex SQL or hundreds of manual Excel formulas. GroupBy is the urban data analyst's superpower.

content.text: 📖 Reading Note: Beyond Matplotlib, the Seaborn library (built on top of Matplotlib) produces better-looking statistical charts with less code. For urban heatmaps — like a grid of all 50 wards showing average PM2.5 levels — sns.heatmap(pm25_pivot, cmap='Reds', annot=True) creates a color-coded matrix in one line. The 'Reds' colormap intuitively shows dangerous zones in dark red. Folium is another essential library: it renders interactive OpenStreetMap-based maps directly from Pandas DataFrames — perfect for urban geospatial visualization.
Definition: EDA is the process of understanding data before applying models.
Goal: Identify trends, detect anomalies, prepare data for ML.

📖 Reading Note: EDA often reveals surprising urban insights. When researchers performed EDA on Mumbai's taxi ridership data, they discovered two distinct peaks instead of one in the morning rush: 7:30am (office workers) and 9:15am (school drop-off parents). This bimodal distribution was invisible in summary statistics but obvious in a histogram. This EDA finding directly influenced MMRDA's school zone traffic regulation policy — no bus pick-ups during 7:00-8:00am in dense residential zones. EDA before modeling is never optional.
Definition: Dashboards are interactive visual interfaces that display data insights.

📖 Reading Note: India's Integrated Command and Control Centres (ICCC) under Smart Cities Mission use Tableau dashboards. The Surat Smart City ICCC dashboard integrates: flood sensor readings (IoT), 311 citizen complaints (crowdsourced), CCTV alerts (AI), and utility consumption data — all in one screen. City administrators can click on any ward on the map and see all active alerts on-screen. Plotly Dash (Python) is the open-source equivalent — you can build a similar dashboard locally with free tools, which is exactly what the project component of Urban Informatics courses target.
End-to-End Process: Load data (Pandas) → Clean data → Analyze (Stats, filtering) → Visualize (Matplotlib) → Present (Dashboard).

content.text: How Week 5 Concepts Connect Across the Course:

rows: scikit-learn's ML algorithms accept Pandas DataFrames as input — Pandas is the universal data format across the ML pipeline
Static Matplotlib charts are the building block; Week 12 scales this to interactive, live dashboards using Plotly/Dash or Tableau
EDA is a mandatory precursor to any ML model — it determines which features to keep, what transformations are needed, and whether the data is clean enough
Week 12's smart city command centers use the exact same dashboard architecture introduced in Week 5, but with real-time IoT data feeds
Understanding data distribution (mean, variance, outliers) from Week 5 is required to interpret clustering results and PCA component importance in Week 8
Lists, dicts, and tuples from Week 4 are the in-memory counterparts of Pandas Series/DataFrames — Week 5 upgrades Week 4 structures for data analysis scale

content.text: 🔗 Big Picture: Week 5 is the 'insight layer' — it sits directly between raw data management (Weeks 2–4) and intelligent prediction (Weeks 6–9). Every ML model you build in Weeks 6–9 begins with exactly the EDA workflow you learn in Week 5. If you skip EDA, your models will be blind to data quality issues.
